metadata.synopsis: The SJC sustained a complaint against Philadelphia Presbytery for failing to judge and record TE Larry Smith’s stated difference over the continuation of prophecy and tongues beyond the apostolic era. The record showed Presbytery approved Smith’s transfer exam and defeated a motion to find his view out of accord, but it did not categorize that view in Smith’s own words. The SJC remanded for a written statement and Presbytery’s categorical judgment, without undoing Smith’s transfer or deciding whether his view was erroneous.

metadata.synopsis: Black challenged Presbytery’s handling of his complaint and its ruling that a licentiate’s non-24-hour creation-day view was not an exception to the Westminster Standards. The SJC denied remand because Presbytery had effectively adjudicated the complaint; the separate objection to proceeding without Black was not first filed below and was administratively out of order. It upheld Presbytery’s ruling that not every non-Calendar-Day view constitutes an exception. Because the record did not identify the licentiate’s precise view, the decision did not determine its acceptability or whether it could be taught.

metadata.synopsis: The complaint challenged James River Presbytery's approval of an ordination examination in which the candidate called the Genesis creation days God's anthropomorphic work days, not necessarily twenty-four-hour days. The complainant argued that view conflicted with WCF I.9. The SJC denied the complaint and answered 'No' to whether the Presbytery erred; the examination stood. It held the Presbytery had authority and discretion, no General Assembly had declared anthropomorphic days contrary to the Standards, and an advisory-committee study left the SJC unwilling to decide creation-day length. A six-member dissent sought an exception and study-committee referral.

metadata.synopsis: Mt. Carmel Session challenged New Jersey Presbytery's creation-days resolution, arguing that the Westminster Standards require six consecutive twenty-four-hour days. The SJC majority concluded that Presbytery could resolve the doctrinal question under BCO 11-4 and that prior Assembly actions permitted latitude on the length of the creation days. The General Assembly rejected the minority report, adopted the majority report, and denied the complaint.
